entry.title: What 26,700 tracks look like to a machine: analysing my music library on a laptop GPU
entry.content:
My music library is mostly Turkish, but not only. There is classical Turkish music from 78 rpm transfers onwards, folk singers with the bağlama, arabesk and Anatolian rock, and around them Persian and Arabic singers, 1980s synth-pop, country, opera, metal and game soundtracks. I had never seen it as a whole, only as a list of folders.

So I ran every track through open-source audio models on my laptop, fetched lyrics for all of them, and used the result twice: to describe the library, and to build playlists from it. No streaming service was involved; the only data that left the laptop were the lyrics lookups.

Tracks

26,707

in about 2,200 albums

Music

1,825 hours

76 days end to end

Size

568 GB

59% of tracks FLAC, 85% of bytes

Distinct recordings

23,687

after merging duplicates

Artists

about 400

20 of them fill half of the hours

Tracks with lyrics

15,231

57%, in at least 10 languages

How the data was made

The analysis is done by AudioMuse-AI, an open-source project that works next to a media server, here Navidrome. Both run in Docker on a laptop with an RTX A5000 Laptop GPU (16 GB). For every track AudioMuse decodes the audio and runs two models:

  • MusiCNN, a small network trained on tagged Western music. It gives a 200-value embedding and scores for 50 tags such as rock, jazz, folk or female vocalists.
  • CLAP, trained on audio paired with text. It gives a 512-value embedding in the same space as text, so the library can be searched with a sentence. AudioMuse also uses it to score six moods: danceable, aggressive, happy, party, relaxed and sad.

With three workers in parallel the full run took 13 hours 23 minutes, about 33 tracks a minute. The models ran on the GPU; decoding stayed on the CPU, which was the real limit. AudioMuse also recognises identical recordings and merges them, so a song that appears on an album and on two compilations counts once.

Lyrics came from LRCLIB, a free, community-run database of synced lyrics, saved as .lrc files next to each track. A few things I learned on the way, useful if you try the same:

  • /api/get searches external sources when a track is not in the database and, under load, returns 503 most of the time. /api/get-cached only looks in the database and answers at once. Ask that first.
  • /api/search often answers 503 with Retry-After: 1. Waiting exactly that second and retrying, instead of an exponential backoff, took my script from 2 to about 25 tracks a minute.
  • Accept a result only if title and artist match after normalisation and the duration is within 2 seconds. Synced lyrics belong to one recording; a live version or a remix of the same song needs different timestamps.
  • Check your own tags first. 843 of my misses had no artist tag or had the file name as the title, so the search was for [Unknown Artist] or 07. Ceza - Kolay Gelsin. Retrying with the folder name as the artist found lyrics for almost half of them.

To compare lyrics, AudioMuse turns them into a vector with the GTE multilingual base model. It ships an int8 version and pins it to the CPU. I compared the available versions on 40 lyrics from the library:

Version Time per track Cosine similarity to fp32 (mean / lowest)
int8, CPU (bundled) 85 to 102 ms 0.949 / 0.891
fp16, GPU 7 to 8 ms 0.957 / 0.912
fp32, GPU 8 to 11 ms 1.000 / 1.000

Both the bundled int8 model and fp16 move the vectors noticeably away from fp32, and fp32 on a GPU is just as fast, so I used fp32.

What is in the library

To describe the library I needed groups that mean something for this music. Tag-based genres do not work here (more on that below), so I grouped by sound: k-means on the combined CLAP and MusiCNN embeddings gave 60 clusters, and I sorted those by hand into nine families by looking at the artists in each.

Classical Turkish music is the largest family by hours, but it has fewer tracks than pop: a sanat müziği recording often runs six or seven minutes, a remix of a dance hit three. The extreme case is Kani Karaca, a hafız whose 173 recordings of hymns and recitations add up to 78 hours, an average of 27 minutes each.

Zeki Müren alone is 110 hours, 6% of the whole library. Inna is second, mostly because of remixes: 1,270 tracks for an artist with a few hundred songs.

This chart says more about how music is published than about when it was recorded. Only 34 tracks are tagged before 1950, although a large part of the classical Turkish collection was recorded on 78 rpm records in the 1930s to 1950s. Those recordings reached me through CD and digital reissues, so their year is the reissue year: the median year of the classical Turkish family is 2004. The 2010s peak is the same effect plus actual new music, deluxe editions and remix albums. If you want the recording date of old music, the tags are not the place to look.

A map of the library

The embeddings have 712 dimensions. UMAP squeezes them into two so that recordings that sound alike end up close together. Every dot is one recording, coloured by family; the labels mark some of the 60 clusters.

The map runs roughly from old to new and from acoustic to electronic. Classical Turkish music fills the left, and its far edge is a cluster where Münir Nurettin Selçuk sits next to 1920s American bands and singers (Fletcher Henderson, Eddie Cantor) and the old records from the BioShock soundtrack. What they share is the sound of shellac, not the music. Folk is next to it, arabesk and Middle Eastern pop in the middle, pop and synth-pop on the right. Two groups are islands of their own: rap at the top, and Wagner with the Vienna Philharmonic at the bottom. Nothing else in the library sounds like an orchestra playing Götterdämmerung.

Lyrics: who is covered and in which language

LRCLIB is excellent for some music and nearly empty for other music. Broken down by family, the difference is large:

Three out of four country, chanson and songwriter tracks have lyrics, most of them synced. For classical Turkish music it is one in six, for folk one in three. In the first pass 12,713 tracks got an .lrc file, and a second pass over the misses, with cleaned-up names and plain lyrics allowed for remixes and live versions, finds about one more in four. The old Turkish repertoire is largely missing from it.

Turkish and English make up 86% of the tracks that have lyrics. Persian is almost entirely Googoosh, Arabic mostly Nancy Ajram and Fairuz, Hebrew mostly Ninet Tayeb. Most of the Spanish is Inna, who recorded a whole Spanish album.

What the models hear

MusiCNN was trained on tags from Last.fm users, mostly for Western music. For every track I took its highest-scoring tag:

Where the music is Western, the tags are fine: rock is rock, country is country, scores are ambient. Where it is not, the model reaches for the nearest thing it knows. Turkish song and arabesk is "rock" for almost half of its tracks. Classical Turkish music is jazz or rock for one track in five each, and blues for one in six. Folk does get "folk", but only for two tracks in five. None of this is wrong in the model's own terms, it just has no word for makam. This matters for any tool that names or samples playlists by these tags, and AudioMuse does both, which is why its own playlists for this library ended up called Rock_Pop_Electronic_Medium_Happy_Party.

The mood scores come from CLAP instead. They all sit in a narrow range, so the chart shows how far each family is from the library average, in standard deviations:

Most of it is what you would expect, which is a good sign: pop is the most danceable and party-like, scores are the least happy, the psychedelic and world group is the most relaxed. Two results I did not expect. Country and chanson come out as the saddest family, ahead of arabesk, whose reputation is built on sadness. And Turkish folk is the least relaxed family in the library. A likely reason for the second: a lot of it is a single voice and a bağlama played hard, close to the microphone.

I left the key estimates out. The analysis reports a key and major or minor for every track, but makam music is not built on major and minor scales, so for half of this library the answer would be forced.

From the data to playlists

AudioMuse builds playlists by clustering a sample of the library and keeping the best-scoring clusters. That is a fine way to suggest a few playlists, but it does not cover a library: asking for 50 playlists gave 1,871 songs out of 23,687. With the genre problem on top, I made the playlists from the same 60 clusters as above:

  • For each cluster, the recordings sorted by distance to the centre, so the most typical ones come first; at most 8 songs per artist, at most 100 songs, and the same song from another album is skipped.
  • Artist radios for the 30 artists with the most tracks: the average of all their vectors, then the closest recordings, at most 15 from the artist and 5 from anyone else. The Cem Karaca radio brings in Erkin Koray, Moğollar and David Bowie, the Googoosh radio Nesrin Sipahi, Fairuz and Nilüfer.
  • 20 themes written as English sentences for CLAP. "1980s synthpop with analog synthesizers" returns OMD, The Human League and Münchener Freiheit. "Sad turkish arabesque with string orchestra" returned film scores by Abel Korzeniowski and Inon Zur: strings and sadness, but none of the arabesk in the library. CLAP has the same blind spot as MusiCNN.

Each playlist is an .m3u8 file in a folder at the root of the library, with paths relative to that folder (../Artist/Album/track.flac), so the same files work on the laptop and on the phone's copy of the library. A short script gives each one a cover made from its four most frequent albums.

The names are Turkish because the library is: Küme is cluster, Radyo radio and Tema theme. Lyrics are not used in these playlists yet. The lyrics vectors mostly encode language and subject, so they will get their own set, grouped by language and by topic.

All settings
  • AudioMuse-AI 3.6.4 (latest-nvidia image), Navidrome 0.64.2, PostgreSQL 15; three analysis workers; ONNX Runtime with the CUDA provider; Whisper off.
  • Analysis: 26,705 files, 48,203 s; 23,687 distinct recordings.
  • LRCLIB: /api/get-cached with title, artist, album and rounded duration, then /api/search with the title without parentheses for the track artist and the album artist. Accepted if normalised title and artist match and the duration differs by at most 2 s; synced lyrics preferred. Three threads, honouring Retry-After.
  • Lyrics vectors: GTE multilingual base, fp32 ONNX export from onnx-community on Hugging Face, first-token pooling, unit length, at most 512 tokens.
  • Clusters: CLAP (512) and 0.7 × MusiCNN (200), each mean-centred and scaled to unit length; RAPIDS cuML KMeans, k = 60, 5 initialisations. Families assigned to clusters by hand.
  • Map: cuML UMAP, cosine metric, 30 neighbours, minimum distance 0.25, same vectors.
  • Moods: AudioMuse's CLAP-based scores; family mean minus library mean, divided by the library standard deviation.
  • Languages: Arabic, Hebrew, Cyrillic and Greek script by character ranges, Persian against Arabic by letters such as پ, چ, گ and ی; Latin-script languages by counting frequent short words; at least 40 letters and 5 matches.
  • Years: album year tag, otherwise the year in the folder name.

entry.title: Restoring the NAO Istanbul recording, part 2: the AI version
Restoring a phone recording of the National Arab Orchestra in Istanbul
entry.content:
On 27 September 2026, during its first visit to Turkey, the National Arab Orchestra played at the opera hall of the Atatürk Kültür Merkezi in Istanbul as part of the Kültür Yolu Festivali. Michael Ibrahim conducted, and the soloists were Nai Barghouti, Usama Baalbaki and, as a guest, the kanun player Aytaç Doğan.

I recorded the whole evening on my phone: 2 hours 10 minutes of mono AAC at 48 kHz and 288 kbps. When I played it back at home it was clearly the concert, but it sounded like it was coming from the next room. This post is about how I turned that file into a 17-track live album. Everything here is ordinary signal processing: measuring, one carefully chosen filter, level control and a lot of cutting.

What was wrong with it

Before changing anything I measured the file.

The good news was that the recording was not damaged. The level was healthy, the hall was quiet while the orchestra played, and only 1,456 samples in more than two hours touched full scale, almost all of them inside applause. The first 14 minutes were the audience finding their seats, which would simply be cut.

The bad news was the tone. Compared with a normal orchestral recording, everything from about 1 kHz upward was too quiet, by 7 dB at 2 kHz, 10 dB at 4 kHz and 12 dB at 5 kHz. Above about 6.5 kHz there was nothing left at all, only the noise floor. My best guess is that the phone was in a pocket or a bag for most of the concert and the fabric ate the high frequencies.

One false alarm on the way: in the first spectrogram I made, there seemed to be a steady line around 1.2 kHz running through the whole recording, and I was ready to notch out a whistle. Tracking the strongest narrow peaks minute by minute showed that the only "constant tones" were at 73, 98, 294 and 392 Hz, which are D and G, the tonal centres of most of the pieces that night. The 1.2 kHz line wandered from minute to minute. It was music, not interference, and there was nothing to remove.

A reference from the orchestra itself

To fix the tone I needed to know what the recording should sound like. The opening piece of the concert was Wa'id (Promise), a composition by Michael Ibrahim in the samai form, and the orchestra released a studio version of it in 2025. The same piece played by the same orchestra is about as good a reference as you can get: the instruments, the arrangement and the melodic range are the same, so any difference in the average spectrum mostly comes from the recording chain, not from the music.

For both versions I computed the long-term average spectrum (Welch's method, 8192-point FFT at 48 kHz) over the loudest 60% of two-second blocks, so that pauses and applause would not pull the average down. I then set both curves to 0 dB at 200 to 400 Hz so that only their shape is compared.

Below 1 kHz the two curves agree within a few dB. Above it the phone falls away faster and faster, and above 6.5 kHz it flattens out at the noise floor while the studio recording carries on.

The difference between the two curves is the correction. I smoothed it to one-octave resolution, so that it follows the broad loss of the recording chain and not individual notes. As a cross-check I repeated the measurement with the orchestra's 2023 concert at the Kennedy Center's Millennium Stage against the whole of my recording, and got almost the same curve; the final correction is the average of the two. Then three limits:

  • no more than +12 dB anywhere;
  • no more than +6 dB below 90 Hz, where boosting mostly brings up handling noise and rumble;
  • above 5.5 kHz the correction fades to zero at 7.5 kHz. There is no music up there to bring back, so boosting it would only make the hiss louder.

I applied it as a linear-phase FIR filter with 8191 taps, together with a 30 Hz high-pass, over the entire recording. A linear-phase filter shifts all frequencies by the same delay, so after removing that delay the corrected file lines up sample for sample with the original.

Data table for figures 1 to 3
Frequency Phone (raw) Studio release Corrected Correction
100 Hz +3.1 dB +3.2 dB +2.2 dB -0.7 dB
252 Hz -4.4 dB -1.6 dB -3.9 dB +0.2 dB
504 Hz -7.2 dB -4.0 dB -6.0 dB +1.2 dB
1.0 kHz -16.1 dB -10.7 dB -11.1 dB +5.0 dB
2.0 kHz -25.8 dB -18.5 dB -17.3 dB +8.3 dB
2.9 kHz -30.8 dB -19.8 dB -21.9 dB +8.6 dB
4.0 kHz -35.5 dB -25.9 dB -25.2 dB +10.6 dB
5.1 kHz -41.9 dB -29.7 dB -30.9 dB +12.0 dB
6.4 kHz -54.6 dB -31.6 dB -47.9 dB +6.6 dB
8.1 kHz -58.4 dB -36.7 dB -60.3 dB +0.0 dB
10.2 kHz -57.5 dB -41.2 dB -59.8 dB +0.0 dB

Level

The second change was level. I used gentle compression (1.8:1 above −26 dB, 30 ms attack, 400 ms release) to bring the quiet passages a little closer to the loud ones, set the integrated loudness to −14 LUFS and put a limiter on the peaks, which in practice only touches the applause. The file is mono and plays on two speakers, so loudness is measured as dual mono.

Integrated loudness

−14.1 LUFS

from −15.5 LUFS

Loudness range

7.3 LU

from 9.5 LU

True peak

−0.6 dBTP

from +2.6 dBTP

The original file was not very quiet to begin with; the bigger change is in the peaks. The phone's AAC decoder produces true peaks up to 2.6 dB over full scale, which can click on some playback chains. After limiting they stay below 0 dBTP, and the loudness range drops only from 9.5 to 7.3 LU, so the orchestra still breathes.

Finding the songs

A two-hour file is not an album. I needed track boundaries and, where possible, titles. Four sources helped.

Audience videos on YouTube. Other people in the hall had uploaded clips, and I had already downloaded eleven of them. I located each one inside my recording with GCC-PHAT, a cross-correlation that whitens the spectrum so two different phones in two different seats still line up. Each clip was tested with three 20-second pieces; when at least two of them pointed to the same offset, the clip was found. Nine of the eleven matched, which gave me Wahashtini, Shuruq, Kaybolan Yıllar, Alışamadım and Ah İstanbul. The other two, Alf Leila wa Leila and Li Beirut, matched nothing, and their descriptions explained why: they were filmed at the second Istanbul concert on 28 September.

Speech recognition for the stage announcements. Whisper did well on the conductor's English: the welcome, the introductions ("our first singer for the evening, the NAO's very own co-founder", Usama Baalbaki; Nai Barghouti "all the way from Palestine"; and for Aytaç Doğan "the most brilliant kanun player", which it heard as "combo player") and the thank-yous at the end. On sung Arabic recorded from the audience it was useless. It filled the gaps with the boilerplate it learned from subtitled YouTube videos, "subscribe to the channel" and "subtitles by" in several languages.

Audience versus stage. I also separated the audience sound (applause, clapping along, talking) from the stage sound with a source-separation model and compared the two levels second by second. (More about that model in part 2.) That gave a clean map of where each piece ends and the applause begins.

Melody matching for the encore. The last piece had no video from my night. Later I found a 47-second clip from the second night titled Kara Köprü Narlıktır. Since it was a different performance, exact alignment was impossible, so I compared melodies instead: 24-bin chroma features (quarter-tone resolution, which Arabic music needs), slid along the whole recording while allowing the tempo to differ by −20% to +30%. The whole clip and each of its halves landed between 127:25 and 129:45, all inside the final four minutes.

The cutting rule was simple: applause belongs to the piece it follows, and spoken introductions go at the start of the piece they introduce. Long speeches got their own tracks.

Cleaning up

Besides the 14 minutes before the concert, there were two places where we were talking in our seats during applause, at 89:40 and 101:42. Each was about 16 to 18 seconds long, and each sat right next to a stretch of clean applause of the same length, so I replaced the talking with that applause, with short crossfades. The last few seconds of the file, where I start speaking again, are faded out.

One thing stayed in. In Şaşkın, during a short break in the music, someone near me shouts an Arabic word of praise, something like "teslem yâ…" ("bless you"). It is the kind of response the conductor had asked for at the beginning of the concert, in the tradition of tarab. I tried turning it down and patching it with the quiet moment before it, and both versions sounded worse than the shout.

Before and after

All clips below are 20 seconds long and matched to the same loudness, so the louder one does not win by default.

Wa'id, phone recording

Wa'id, corrected

Ah İstanbul, phone recording

Ah İstanbul, corrected

What the correction cannot do: it cannot bring back what was never recorded. There is still nothing above about 7 kHz, so cymbals and the air of the hall stay dull, and the recording is still mono. The result sounds like a decent broadcast from an old radio, which is a long way from where it started.

The album

Seventeen tracks, 1 hour 56 minutes. Three titles are still unknown to me; if you were there and recognise them, please write to me.

The album is in this folder as 24-bit / 48 kHz FLAC: National Arab Orchestra, Istanbul, 27 September 2026.

Part 2 is about a second version of the album, made with two machine-learning models. That version is in its own folder.

This is an audience recording made for personal listening. The music belongs to the National Arab Orchestra, the soloists and the composers. If any of them would like it taken down, email me and I will remove it.
